Action Plan:
1. Arrange same-day face-to-face clinic assessment (GP/ENT) for left-sided hearing reduction — perform focused neurological cranial nerve examination and otoscopy; if available, perform bedside tuning‑fork testing and refer for formal audiology (pure‑tone audiometry) urgently.  
2. Arrange further diagnostics if indicated after clinical exam: urgent audiometry and consider MRI brain with internal auditory meatus / cerebellopontine angle protocol if compressive lesion (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) suspected.  
3. Assess left-sided facial numbness at the in-person visit to determine distribution (sensory vs motor), document presence/absence of facial weakness or vesicular rash, and use findings to guide further management (e.g., urgent imaging or ENT/neuro referral).  
4. Evaluate intermittent tinnitus and dizziness during clinic visit; document severity and occupational impact (jockey). Provide temporary work/activity advice based on clinical findings (no specific work restriction provided remotely).  
5. Administrative actions: clinician will message admin to book a same‑day clinic slot; patient instructed to call the support team number (left in notes) ~5 minutes after booking request so they can be slotted into a convenient clinic. Patient to ensure appointment attended today.  
6. No new medications or treatments were initiated remotely; treatment decisions (e.g., steroids or antiviral) will follow in-person assessment and documented findings.  
7. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Progressive reduced hearing and facial numbness on the left side for ~3 weeks.
- History of presenting illness:
  - Onset: ~3 weeks ago, persistent.
  - Symptoms: Left-sided decreased hearing; left-sided facial numbness localized around left ear and along left jawline; occasional tinnitus (ringing) and intermittent dizziness associated with ringing. Symptoms ongoing and impacting work/training.
  - No ear discharge, no ear pain, no fever.
  - No reported limb weakness, swallowing difficulty, speech difficulty, or visual disturbance.
- Past medical history:
  - Nasal polyps (intermittent), uses a prescribed nasal spray as needed (name not recalled).
  - Remote history reportedly of "labyrinthitis" (patient unsure of details).
- Medications:
  - Intermittent nasal steroid spray (prescription — name not documented; dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Occasional antacid (Rennies).
- Allergies:
  - Latex.
- Family history:
  - Brother with neurofibromatosis (type not specified).
- Social history:
  - Occupation: jockey (working; symptoms affecting ability to train).
  - Lives with partner. No pets. Smoking/alcohol not documented.

Objective:
- No physical exam or vital signs documented (video consultation only).
- Plan documented by clinician: arrange in-person focused neurological and ear examination and otoscopy today.
- No investigations/results available at time of consult.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Left-sided hearing reduction:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Sensorineural or conductive hearing loss to be determined on exam/audiometry (definitive diagnosis pending). DDx support: Vestibular schwannoma — Medium-High likelihood (DDx item: "Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)", Medium-High); Labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis — Medium (DDx item: "Labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis", Medium).  
   - Differential diagnosis (from DDx, where consistent):
     - Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) — Medium-High (supporting: unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, family history NF; opposing: relatively short 3‑week history and no objective audiometry yet).
     - Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis — Medium (supporting: prior history; opposing: facial numbness not typical).
     - Ramsay Hunt syndrome / Bell's palsy-type processes — Low-Medium (supporting: ipsilateral ear symptoms; opposing: no facial weakness or rash documented).
     - Brainstem lesion (e.g., AICA infarct) — Low (supporting: combined cranial nerve symptoms possible; opposing: subacute course, absence of other neurological deficits).
   - Investigations planned:
     - Urgent face-to-face otoscopic and neurological cranial nerve exam today.
     - Urgent audiology referral for pure‑tone audiometry and speech audiometry.
     - Consider MRI brain with internal auditory meatus / CPA protocol if clinical exam or audiometry suggest a sensorineural pattern or compressive lesion.
   - Treatment planned:
     - No medications started remotely. Treatment decisions (steroids, antivirals, etc.) to be made after in-person assessment and investigations.
   - Referrals:
     - ENT and/or neurology referral as indicated by findings; audiology arranged urgently.

2. Left-sided facial numbness:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Focal cranial sensory disturbance — etiologic diagnosis pending (assessment will determine sensory vs motor involvement). DDx support: Vestibular schwannoma — Medium-High (if compressive spread) and Ramsay Hunt/Bell's palsy-type processes — Low-Medium (DDx items cited).  
   - Differential diagnosis (from DDx, where consistent):
     - Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) — Medium-High (supporting: ipsilateral sensory changes; opposing: facial numbness without other objective deficits yet).
     - Ramsay Hunt syndrome / Bell's palsy-type processes — Low-Medium (supporting: possible cranial nerve involvement; opposing: patient reports numbness not motor weakness and no vesicular rash).
     - Brainstem lesion (vascular or demyelinating) — Low (possible but less likely given subacute course and lack of other focal deficits).
     - Multiple sclerosis / demyelinating disease — considered but less likely (DDx item "Multiple sclerosis" listed); requires further evaluation if other signs develop.
   - Investigations planned:
     - Neurological cranial nerve examination during in-person visit to document sensory distribution and motor function (including facial motor testing).
     - Further imaging (MRI) if exam suggests central or compressive lesion.
   - Treatment planned:
     - No treatment initiated remotely; management determined after examination and investigations.
   - Referrals:
     - ENT ± neurology and imaging as indicated.

3. Tinnitus and intermittent dizziness with occupational impact:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Tinnitus and intermittent vestibular symptoms likely related to same underlying ear/CPA process or peripheral vestibular pathology (diagnosis pending). DDx support: Labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis — Medium; Vestibular schwannoma — Medium-High; Ramsay Hunt — Low-Medium.  
   - Differential diagnosis (from DDx, where consistent):
     - Labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis — Medium.
     - Vestibular schwannoma — Medium-High.
     - Ramsay Hunt syndrome — Low-Medium.
     - Ototoxicity, middle ear pathology, vascular/brainstem causes — lower likelihood per DDx but considered if history/exam suggests.
   - Investigations planned:
     - Document symptoms in clinic; bedside vestibular testing as appropriate.
     - Audiometry and vestibular testing as indicated; consider MRI if clinical suspicion for CPA lesion.
   - Treatment planned:
     - No remote treatment; symptomatic management and occupational advice to be provided after assessment.
   - Referrals:
     - ENT/audiology and neurology referral as indicated.

  - Smoking, alcohol use, and pregnancy status not documented.
  - Support team phone number was to be left in notes but is not present in the transcript.

Both perspectives are documented; further in-person exam and investigations are required to reconcile.
